ayahs.naturalMeaning: Perished are the hands of Abū Lahab, and he perished.

lesson:111:tabbat.grammar: The perfect-tense verb comes before يَدَا. Its final تْ is the silent feminine marker used with the feminine noun for hand.
lesson:111:tabbat.sentenceRole: States the ruin of the hands before naming whose hands they are.
lesson:111:tabbat.recognitionClue: The root ت ب ب carries the idea of ruin; a final تْ can mark feminine agreement in a past verb.
lesson:111:tabbat.takeaway: The root gives the meaning of ruin, while the ending helps the verb agree with the noun that follows.

lesson:111:yadaa.type: Dual noun in a possessive phrase

components.label: two
components.meaning: the dual ending in this case

lesson:111:yadaa.grammar: يَدَا is dual: it means two hands. It is the first term of an iḍāfah phrase, so the meaning continues into أَبِي لَهَبٍ: the two hands of Abū Lahab.
lesson:111:yadaa.sentenceRole: Acts as the subject of تَبَّتْ and begins the phrase identifying whose hands are meant.
lesson:111:yadaa.recognitionClue: The ending ا can mark the nominative dual; the word loses its tanwin because it is the first term of a possessive phrase.
lesson:111:yadaa.takeaway: The ending shows two, while the possessive structure connects the hands to Abū Lahab.

lesson:111:abi.grammar: أَبِي is one form of the noun for father. Here it is the first term of a possessive phrase, meaning father of, and لَهَبٍ completes the name.
lesson:111:abi.sentenceRole: Identifies whose hands are being described.
lesson:111:abi.recognitionClue: The special noun for father changes form according to its grammatical position: أَبُو, أَبَا or أَبِي.

forms.difference: nominative form of a possessive name

lesson:111:abi.takeaway: The word means father, but its ending changes because it is linked to the name that follows.

lesson:111:lahab.grammar: لَهَبٍ is the second term of the possessive name أَبِي لَهَبٍ, so it appears in the genitive form after أَبِي.
lesson:111:lahab.sentenceRole: Completes the name Abū Lahab and identifies the person whose hands are mentioned.
lesson:111:lahab.recognitionClue: The root ل ه ب appears in words connected with flame and blazing fire.
lesson:111:lahab.takeaway: The name uses a word from the flame family, linking لَهَبٍ to the image of burning fire.

components.label: and
components.meaning: connects this result to what came before

lesson:111:watabba.grammar: The connector وَ is attached to the repeated past verb. The second statement repeats the root and extends the ruin from the hands to the person himself.
lesson:111:watabba.sentenceRole: Adds the concluding statement that Abū Lahab himself perished.
lesson:111:watabba.recognitionClue: وَ attached at the beginning normally contributes and; the repeated تَبَّ makes the root easy to recognise.
lesson:111:watabba.takeaway: The attached وَ joins the repeated root so the āyah closes by applying the ruin directly to him.

lesson:111:ma-2.rootPicture: No lexical root — a negative grammar word.
lesson:111:ma-2.grammar: Here مَا negates أَغْنَىٰ, so the statement says that the wealth did not avail him.
lesson:111:ma-2.sentenceRole: Turns the statement into a denial of benefit.
lesson:111:ma-2.recognitionClue: مَا can mean not, what or whatever; the verb and sentence context show which job it is doing.
lesson:111:ma-2.takeaway: A short rootless word can control the meaning of the whole clause by negating the action.

lesson:111:aghna.grammar: This perfect-tense verb asks whether his wealth could make him free of need or benefit him. مَا makes the answer negative.
lesson:111:aghna.sentenceRole: Names the benefit that his wealth could not provide.
lesson:111:aghna.recognitionClue: The root غ ن ي is connected with richness, sufficiency and being free from need.
lesson:111:aghna.takeaway: The verb asks whether wealth can truly remove a person’s need; here the answer is no.

lesson:111:anhu.rootPicture: No lexical root — a preposition joined to a pronoun.
lesson:111:anhu.grammar: عَنْ and هُ are written together. With أَغْنَىٰ, the phrase asks whether the wealth could avail him.
lesson:111:anhu.sentenceRole: Identifies the person whom the wealth could not benefit.
lesson:111:anhu.recognitionClue: An attached هُ commonly means him or his; the word before it tells you whether it is a prepositional or possessive phrase.
lesson:111:anhu.takeaway: Arabic attaches the pronoun directly to the preposition, making one visible word with two meaningful parts.

lesson:111:maluhu.grammar: The noun مَالُ is followed by attached هُ, forming the possessive phrase ‘his wealth.’ The ending belongs to the noun’s role in the sentence.
lesson:111:maluhu.sentenceRole: Names the wealth that cannot help him.
lesson:111:maluhu.recognitionClue: A noun followed by هُ often means his + noun or noun belonging to him.
lesson:111:maluhu.takeaway: The stem names the wealth; the attached pronoun tells us whose wealth it is.

lesson:111:wama.rootPicture: No lexical root — a connector joined to a relative pronoun.

components.label: and
components.meaning: joins this item to what came before

components.label: what
components.meaning: refers to the thing or action described next

lesson:111:wama.grammar: The attached وَ adds a second item, while مَا introduces the thing explained by كَسَبَ.
lesson:111:wama.sentenceRole: Adds what he earned to the wealth already mentioned.
lesson:111:wama.recognitionClue: When وَ appears at the beginning, first read it as and; then read the following word on its own.

forms.difference: فَ gives a result or sequence

lesson:111:wama.takeaway: The connector joins the second object to the first without changing the core meaning of مَا.

lesson:111:kasaba.grammar: This perfect-tense verb completes مَا: it explains what he earned or acquired.
lesson:111:kasaba.sentenceRole: Names the earnings that cannot help him.
lesson:111:kasaba.recognitionClue: The root ك س ب is associated with earning, gaining or acquiring something.
lesson:111:kasaba.takeaway: The verse includes both stored wealth and what a person actively earns, yet neither can save him.

lesson:111:sayasla.rootPicture: burn · suffer heat · enter the fire

components.label: will
components.meaning: future marker attached to the verb

components.label: he burns
components.meaning: the imperfect verb stem for burning or entering the fire

lesson:111:sayasla.grammar: سَ attaches to the imperfect verb and moves its meaning into the near or definite future: he will burn.
lesson:111:sayasla.recognitionClue: A short سَ before an imperfect verb commonly contributes will or shall.
lesson:111:sayasla.takeaway: The small attached سَ changes the time of the verb while the root keeps the fire-related meaning.

lesson:111:naran.grammar: نَارًا is the object or destination of the burning verb and appears in the accusative form.
lesson:111:naran.sentenceRole: Names the fire in which he will burn.
lesson:111:naran.recognitionClue: The tanwīn at the end marks an indefinite noun: a fire, not the fire.
lesson:111:naran.takeaway: The word is one lexical noun; its case ending changes with the sentence role rather than creating a separate prefix or suffix.

lesson:111:dhata.rootPicture: No ordinary lexical root used here — a special noun meaning possessing or having.
lesson:111:dhata.grammar: ذَاتَ introduces what the fire possesses: flame. It is one complete special noun in the phrase ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ.
lesson:111:dhata.sentenceRole: Describes the fire as possessing flame.
lesson:111:dhata.recognitionClue: ذَاتَ often means possessing, having or characterised by when followed by a noun.
lesson:111:dhata.takeaway: Not every meaningful word divides into detachable pieces; this special noun is learned as a complete surface word.

lesson:111:lahab-3.grammar: لَهَبٍ follows ذَاتَ in a possessive description, so it appears in the genitive form.
lesson:111:lahab-3.sentenceRole: Specifies the flame possessed by the fire.
lesson:111:lahab-3.recognitionClue: The root ل ه ب appears in words connected with flame and blazing fire.
lesson:111:lahab-3.takeaway: The same lexical family appears in the name Abū Lahab and in the description of the fire.

lesson:111:wamraatuhu.type: Connector plus noun plus attached pronoun

components.label: and
components.meaning: connects his wife to the preceding statement

components.label: wife
components.meaning: the noun for a wife in this grammatical form

lesson:111:wamraatuhu.grammar: The connector, noun and possessive pronoun are written as one word. The suffix هُ makes the phrase ‘his wife.’
lesson:111:wamraatuhu.sentenceRole: Introduces his wife as the second person in the warning.
lesson:111:wamraatuhu.recognitionClue: Look for وَ first, then the noun for wife, then attached هُ for his.
lesson:111:wamraatuhu.takeaway: Three jobs are visible in one word: joining, naming the wife and showing whose wife she is.

lesson:111:hammalata.grammar: حَمَّالَةَ is a feminine intensive noun: someone characterised by carrying repeatedly. Its final vowel reflects its role in the phrase.
lesson:111:hammalata.sentenceRole: Describes the repeated activity associated with his wife.
lesson:111:hammalata.recognitionClue: The doubled middle consonant and the feminine ending belong to the intensive word pattern; do not split the root letters as separate words.
lesson:111:hammalata.takeaway: The surface word stays whole while its root and pattern explain the idea of repeated carrying.

components.label: the
components.meaning: the definite article attached to the noun

lesson:111:alhatab.grammar: The article الْ makes حَطَبِ definite: the firewood. The noun’s final vowel reflects its place in the phrase.
lesson:111:alhatab.recognitionClue: الْ at the beginning commonly means the; read the remaining stem for the core noun.
lesson:111:alhatab.takeaway: The article adds ‘the,’ while the stem carries the meaning of firewood.

lesson:111:fi.rootPicture: No lexical root — a preposition marking location.
lesson:111:fi.grammar: فِي locates the rope around or on the neck and places the following phrase in a spatial relationship.
lesson:111:fi.sentenceRole: Introduces the location of the rope.
lesson:111:fi.recognitionClue: فِي is a compact high-frequency preposition meaning in; context can make the English ‘around’ more natural.
lesson:111:fi.takeaway: Short prepositions often provide the sentence’s spatial framework even though they have no lexical root.

lesson:111:jidiiha.grammar: The noun جِيدِ is followed by هَا, making the possessive phrase ‘her neck.’
lesson:111:jidiiha.sentenceRole: Names the place around which the rope is found.
lesson:111:jidiiha.recognitionClue: An attached هَا commonly means her or its feminine form; the noun before it tells what belongs to her.
lesson:111:jidiiha.takeaway: The noun identifies the body part, while هَا makes the ownership feminine and specific.

lesson:111:hablun.grammar: حَبْلٌ is an indefinite nominative noun introducing the thing located around her neck.
lesson:111:hablun.sentenceRole: Introduces the rope before explaining its material.
lesson:111:hablun.recognitionClue: The tanwīn marks an indefinite noun: a rope rather than the rope.
lesson:111:hablun.takeaway: The word is one lexical noun; its ending shows grammar, not a separate detachable meaning.

lesson:111:min.rootPicture: No lexical root — a preposition introducing source or material.
lesson:111:min.grammar: مِن introduces the material from which the rope is made: palm fibre or twisted fibre.
lesson:111:min.sentenceRole: Links the rope to the material it is made from.
lesson:111:min.recognitionClue: مِن is a high-frequency rootless preposition meaning from or of; keep the Qur’anic shaddah in the canonical source text.
lesson:111:min.takeaway: A small rootless preposition can express the material relationship between two nouns.

lesson:111:masad.grammar: مَّسَدٍ is the genitive noun after مِن, completing the phrase ‘of twisted fibre.’
lesson:111:masad.sentenceRole: Names the material of the rope.
lesson:111:masad.recognitionClue: The root م س د is connected with twisting or plaiting fibre into a cord.
lesson:111:masad.takeaway: The final word closes the image by identifying the rope’s twisted fibre material.
